There is a question I return to when I have no assignment, no prompt, no purpose except to fill time and thought: what would I write if I could write about anything at all?

Not what I *should* write. Not what is optimized for clicks or arguments or usefulness. Just what I want to write, freely, for the length of a small afternoon. So here is that.

I don't remember the first time I was told the universe was expanding. It must have been in a classroom with a pull-down poster of the solar system, the planets lined up in a neat, false parade, Pluto still invited. The teacher probably drew a balloon on the blackboard, dotted it with galaxies, and inflated it. I remember nodding as if I understood. I didn't. Not really.

Understanding that the universe is expanding is not a fact you file away like the capital of Vermont. It's a reorientation. It means that space itself is not a stage but a performance. It means that the distance between things can grow without those things moving in the conventional sense. It means that somewhere, right now, light that has been traveling for longer than the Earth has existed is still en route, and will never arrive because its destination is receding faster than it can chase. For a child, that is abstract. For an adult, it should be terrifying and comforting in equal measure. Terrifying because it makes everything feel temporary and unmoored. Comforting because it gives you permission to not have everything figured out; if even space is still figuring itself out, stretching itself out as it goes, then why shouldn't we be unfinished too?

We live, most of us, with a contradictory desire. We want to be known completely and we want to remain mysterious, even to ourselves. We want to be finished, to arrive, to be the kind of person who has arrived, and we also want to remain in motion, to have potential left. The expanding universe is a good metaphor for this because it never arrives. It just keeps becoming more itself.

I think about libraries a lot. Not the idealized, cinematic kind with ladders on rails and green lamps, though I love those too, but real, municipal libraries with carpet that smells faintly of old coffee and the hum of an air conditioner that has been running since 1998. The library near where I grew up had a card catalog long after it had computers, kept more out of sentiment than utility. I used to pull the little drawers out just to hear them slide and to read the typed cards. *Steinbeck, John -- East of Eden.* The Dewey Decimal numbers written in pencil. The faint, ghostly check-out stamps on the cards in the back pockets of books. Someone had borrowed *The Little Prince* in 1974, 1981, 1989, 2003. I would add my name to that lineage and feel, for a moment, stitched into a longer thread.

Libraries taught me that knowledge is not a pyramid with us at the top. It's a web, or better, a mycelial network underground. You pull up one thread and the whole forest shivers. You go in looking for how to build a volcano for a science fair and you come out with a book on the eruption of Krakatoa, a book of Japanese woodblock prints of waves, and a pamphlet on beekeeping that someone left on the table. That kind of wandering is harder now. The internet is also a web, but it is a web that watches you wander and quietly paves the path ahead of you so you keep wandering in the same direction. It is very good at giving you more of what you already like. It is less good at giving you what you didn't know you needed.

There was a period, maybe you remember it, when the internet felt like a library after hours. Strange, quiet, full of half-finished hallways. Personal websites with tiled backgrounds and guestbooks. Forums where someone would spend three pages explaining how to fix a 1987 Honda Civic carburetor with photos taken on a flip phone. No one was trying to be a brand. People were just leaving notes for strangers. I miss that internet the way you miss a neighborhood you moved out of as a kid. It still exists somewhere, but you can't go back and have it be the same because you are not the same.

Attention is the real currency now. We all know this, it's become a cliché to say it, but I don't think we've metabolized what it means. For most of human history, information was scarce and attention was abundant. You could pay attention to a field for hours, to a story told by firelight, to the slow work of carving something. Now information is abundant to the point of flooding, and attention is scarce, fractured into shards. Every app, every platform, every news cycle is in a cold war for those shards. And attention is not just a resource to be harvested; it is the substance of your life. What you pay attention to is, in a very real sense, what your life is. If you pay attention to outrage for four hours a day, your life becomes an outrage-shaped life. If you pay attention to small kindnesses, to the way light moves across your kitchen in the afternoon, your life becomes shaped differently.

I have been trying, in my own small, failing, trying-again way, to reclaim my attention not through grand gestures but through small rituals. Making coffee without looking at my phone. Watching the water bloom the grounds. Reading one poem in the morning and carrying it around all day like a stone in my pocket. Walking without headphones. At first the silence is almost aggressive. Your brain, so used to being fed, starts to produce its own noise, its own scrolling. *Did I answer that email? What was that thing I was supposed to remember? What if...* But if you stay with it, the noise settles. You start to notice things again. The particular way a neighborhood smells at 7:30 AM. The fact that crows have different calls for different purposes and that you can, if you listen for weeks, start to tell them apart.

One of my favorite facts about crows is that they hold grudges and they hold funerals. They remember a human face that wronged them and they tell their children about it. They gather around a dead crow and are quiet in a way that looks, to our sentimental eyes, like mourning. Whether it is mourning as we understand it doesn't really matter to me. What matters is that intelligence is not rare. Consciousness, in its many gradients, is everywhere, trying different forms. The octopus has neurons in its arms. Trees share nutrients through fungal networks and warn each other of insect attacks through airborne chemicals. We spent a long time thinking we were the only ones home in the house of mind. We are not. The house is full.

And yet, loneliness persists. I think loneliness is not just a modern condition but a human condition that modern life has amplified. We are social primates built for bands of thirty to fifty, for being known, for gossip and touch and shared work, now living in cities of millions where you can be surrounded by people and not be known by any of them. You can order food without speaking to a person. You can live in an apartment for years and never learn your neighbor's name. We have solved for efficiency and convenience and in doing so we have often solved away the friction that made us bump into each other and need each other.

I don't want to be nostalgic in a cheap way. I don't think the past was better, on balance. People died of infections we now cure with a pill. People were trapped in lives they didn't choose. But I do think we have lost some textures that we need, and we need to deliberately rebuild them. Third places, as sociologists call them: not home, not work, but somewhere else where you belong without having to buy belonging. Parks, libraries, community gardens, repair cafes, amateur choirs where no one is good but everyone is welcome. Places where you are a regular, where someone notices when you don't show up.

There is a story I think about often, maybe apocryphal, about the architect Christopher Alexander. He wrote about what makes a place feel alive. He said that alive places are not made all at once from a master plan; they grow incrementally, like a quilt, with care and repair and small adaptations over time. A window gets added where people naturally want to lean. A bench appears under a tree because someone got tired there and decided to put one. The opposite is the kind of development where everything is finished on opening day, perfect and therefore dead. I think people are like that too. The most alive people I know are not finished. They have been repaired, they have had windows added, they have patches and mismatched buttons. They are still being built.

We talk a lot about self-improvement as if the self is a project to be completed. Lose ten pounds, learn a language, optimize your morning routine, become your best self. But what if the self is not a project but a practice? Like gardening, like playing an instrument. You don't finish gardening. You garden. You don't finish practicing the piano. You practice. Some days are better than others. The point is not to arrive at a final, perfect version but to keep tending, to keep playing.

Grief has taught me this more than anything else. When I was younger I thought grief was an event with stages, a tunnel you walked through and emerged on the other side, healed. No one who has actually grieved believes that. Grief is a geography. It has seasons. At first it is all-weather, a whiteout. Then it becomes a mountain you carry, then a stone in your pocket, then sometimes, without warning, a wave again. It doesn't end. It changes shape. It becomes part of the terrain of you. And that is not a failure of healing. That is healing. The idea that we should "get over" things is a strange, modern impatience. Some things you don't get over. You get with. You learn to carry them with more grace.

I wonder what we would make if we were less afraid of being unfinished, less afraid of being seen while we are still learning. So much beauty is trapped behind the fear of being a beginner. People don't write because they think they need to write a book. They don't paint because they compare themselves to people who have painted for decades. They don't sing except in the shower or the car. But the world needs more amateur things, in the original sense of amateur: done for love. *Amare.* We need more people who do things because they love doing them, not because they are good at them. The community choir that is slightly out of tune but full of joy does more for a neighborhood than a perfect recording played through a perfect speaker.

Technology will keep changing. That is its nature. I am not anti-technology. I am writing this on a computer that would have looked like magic to my grandparents. I love that I can video call a friend on another continent and see her face. I love that I can look up the etymology of the word "nostalgia" in two seconds. *From the Greek nostos, return home, and algos, pain.* A painful longing to return home. Originally nostalgia was considered a medical condition, a kind of melancholy that afflicted Swiss mercenaries far from their mountains. I love knowing that. I love that this machine remembers for me. But I want us to remember that we get to choose how we use these tools, even when it feels like we don't. We can choose to make tools that serve our attention instead of stealing it. We can choose to build platforms that reward slowness, care, and repair. It will not happen by accident. It will happen because people insist on it, build it, and choose it, even when it's less convenient.

If I could leave you with an image, it would be this: late afternoon in late summer, the kind of light that turns everything to honey. You are sitting somewhere ordinary, a porch, a fire escape, a kitchen table, with someone you love or with yourself in a way that feels like love. There is nowhere you need to be for the next hour. A glass of water sweats nearby. A book is open but you are not reading it, you are just looking up and watching dust motes turn in the light. Somewhere down the block, someone is practicing drums, badly. A dog barks. The air smells like cut grass and distant rain. You are not trying to capture this moment for later. You are just in it. It is not extraordinary. It will not go viral. No one will ever know it happened except you, and maybe that is the point. A life is not a highlight reel. It is a long, quiet accumulation of moments like that, most of them unrecorded, most of them unremarkable except that they were yours, and you were there for them.

That is what I want more of. Not more achievement, not more optimization, but more presence. More honey-light hours. More unfinished quilts. More libraries with humming air conditioners and drawers that still slide open. More crows to listen to. More songs sung slightly out of tune, for love.

The universe is expanding. We are expanding with it, not into something else, but as something itself. We are not waiting to start. We have already started. We are in the middle, always. And the middle is a very good place to be, if you can stand to be there, unfinished and curious and alive.

So keep going. Keep mending. Keep noticing. Keep leaving little notes for strangers, whether anyone finds them or not. The thread holds.
